chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Isma'il ibn Marar, from Yunus, from Ubayd Allah ibn Ali al-Halabi, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said to Umar ibn al-Khattab: 'Three things: if you preserve them and act upon them, they will suffice you for what is besides them; and if you leave them, nothing besides them will benefit you.' He said: 'And what are they, O Abu al-Hasan?' He said: 'Establishing the legal punishments upon the close and the distant, and judging by the Book of Allah in pleasure and in anger, and dividing fairly between the red and the black.' Then Umar said to him: 'By my life, you have indeed been concise and comprehensive.'

key_terms.بَيْنَ الْأَحْمَرِ وَالْأَسْوَدِ: Between the red and the black

ai.seo_question: What are the three key principles of governance emphasized in Shia hadith for leaders?
ai.summary: This narration, found in Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, highlights the continuity of just governance from the era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs to the Imams, with Umar ibn al-Khattab acknowledging the depth of Imam Ali’s concise advice. The three pillars—impartial application of hudud, objective adherence to the Quran amidst bias, and equitable distribution (qasam)—are presented as sufficient for comprehensive leadership. This underscores the Shia scholarly view that the principles of justice articulated by Ali were universally recognized as the foundation of legitimate authority.
